title: Organising a Kilimanjaro Group Climb? Build It Around Your Slowest Walker
meta_title: Kilimanjaro Group Climb Planning for Clubs and Friends
meta_description: Plan a Kilimanjaro group climb: best routes for mixed fitness, guide and porter numbers, current park fees and how to handle summit night together.
excerpt: How to plan a Kilimanjaro group climb for friends, clubs or colleagues: which route suits mixed fitness, how many guides and porters you need, real park fees and a summit-night plan that keeps everyone safe.
content:
A Kilimanjaro group climb works best with four to twelve people on a longer route such as Lemosho, with roughly one guide for every two climbers so the group can split by pace on summit night. Park fees stay the same per person, but shared transport, guides and kitchen crew bring the cost per climber down.

The trouble with organising a climb for friends, a running club or a team from work is that you are not planning for one person. You are planning for the fittest and the slowest, the keen camper and the one who has never slept in a tent. This guide covers routes, crew numbers, real park fees, training and the summit-night plan, so the group arrives in Moshi ready and leaves together.

Photo: Divulge Adventures

Quick Facts

  • Summit: Uhuru Peak, 5,895 m, the highest point in Africa
  • Guiding rule: every climb must be led by a licensed operator; solo trekking is not allowed
  • Best group size: 4-12 climbers per Kilimanjaro group climb crew; larger groups split into two
  • Best months: January to mid-March and June to October, the driest periods
  • Park fees: US$70 a day plus US$50 a night camping and a US$20 rescue fee, plus 18% VAT (checked November 2026)
  • Recommended length: 7-8 days on the mountain for mixed-fitness groups
  • Start point: Moshi, under an hour by road from Kilimanjaro International Airport

What Makes a Kilimanjaro Group Climb Different From Climbing Alone?

A Kilimanjaro group climb is different because the plan has to protect the weakest day of the slowest person, not the best day of the fittest. Pace, rest stops, meals and tent routines are shared, and one person's altitude headache affects everyone's morning.

Photo: Divulge Adventures

That sounds like a drawback, but groups often do better than they expect. People who would have rushed alone are held to the slow, steady walk the guides call "pole pole", and the evening meal in the mess tent becomes the best part of the day. Climbers who start nervous are carried along by the others.

Pace is set by the guides, not the group's fastest walker

On a well-run climb the lead guide walks at the front and sets a pace that feels almost too slow at low altitude. The fastest member of a group rarely likes this on day one, but by the third night, sleeping close to 4,000 m, the reason becomes obvious. Racing ahead early is one of the easiest ways to arrive at Barafu with a headache.

One person's bad day should not end anyone else's climb

The single most important planning decision is having enough guides that someone can descend with a climber who is unwell while the rest carry on. Ask any operator how they handle this on a Kilimanjaro group climb before you book. If the answer is that the whole group turns around, keep looking.

Which Kilimanjaro Route Suits a Group Best?

Lemosho is the route we suggest most often for groups, with seven or eight days on the mountain. It gains height slowly, starts in quiet rainforest and gives slower walkers time to adapt. Machame and Rongai suit fitter groups, while Marangu is the only route with huts.

Route choice for a Kilimanjaro group climb comes down to two questions: how much time can everyone take off, and how mixed is the fitness? A group of marathon runners with a fixed week can manage Machame. A group that includes a 60-year-old, two first-time campers and a colleague who has never walked uphill for more than an hour should be on the longest itinerary the budget allows. Our full comparison of all seven Kilimanjaro routes covers each one in more detail, and the Lemosho versus Machame breakdown helps if your group is torn between the two most popular choices.

RouteDays on the mountainWhy it suits a groupWatch out for
Lemosho7-8Slow height gain, quiet forest start, plenty of time for slower walkers to adaptLonger and dearer; long drive to Londorossi Gate
Machame6-7Scenic, popular, good climb-high-sleep-low profile on the Lava Tower dayBusy camps in peak months; the 6-day version is tight for mixed groups
Rongai6-7Quieter northern approach, gentler gradient, drier side in the shoulder monthsLong transfer to Nalemuru Gate; less varied scenery
Marangu5-6Huts at Mandara, Horombo and Kibo suit groups that dislike campingHut places must be booked ahead; the short version leaves little time to acclimatise

One point organisers of a Kilimanjaro group climb often miss: the extra day is cheaper than it looks. A day on the mountain adds one day of fees, crew wages and food per person, but it is the single biggest thing that improves your chance of everyone reaching the summit together.

How Many Guides, Porters and Tents Does a Group Need?

A common benchmark among responsible operators is about one guide for every two climbers, counting the lead guide and assistants, plus roughly three or four porters per climber on camping routes. A group of eight therefore climbs with a crew of around 30 people.

Photo by World Wanderer on Unsplash

Those numbers surprise anyone organising a first Kilimanjaro group climb, but every piece of a group's camp has to be carried: sleeping tents, a mess tent with table and chairs, toilet tents, the kitchen, food for a week and water. The Kilimanjaro Porters Assistance Project sets a load limit of 20 kg per porter for company gear, not counting the porter's own kit, which is why porter numbers rise with group size.

Kilimanjaro group climb crew in numbers

The table below is a planning guide, not a fixed formula. Exact numbers depend on the route, the length of the climb and how much comfort kit you want, such as a larger mess tent or a private toilet tent for each pair.

Group sizeGuides (lead plus assistants)Porters (rough guide)Tents
4 climbers2-312-162 sleeping tents, mess tent, toilet tent
8 climbers4-524-324 sleeping tents, 1-2 mess tents, 2 toilet tents
12 climbers6-736-486 sleeping tents, 2 mess tents, 2-3 toilet tents
16+ climbers8 or more, in two crews48 or moreSplit into two camps a short walk apart

Rooming on the mountain

On a Kilimanjaro group climb most people share two to a sleeping tent. Decide early who shares with whom, and tell your operator if anyone wants a single tent, as it usually adds a porter and a supplement. Snorers are a real issue at altitude, where everyone sleeps lightly anyway, so it is worth asking the question honestly.

How Much Does a Kilimanjaro Group Climb Cost Per Person?

The cost of a Kilimanjaro group climb starts with park fees of around US$800-1,100 per adult, depending on route length, and those fees do not fall with group size. What does fall is each person's share of transfers, guides, cooks and camp kit.

The fees below come from the Tanzania National Parks tariff for adult non-residents, checked in November 2026. Children aged 5 to 15 pay lower rates. Fees and VAT treatment do change, so confirm the current figures on the official Kilimanjaro National Park visitor guide or with us before you set a fundraising target or collect deposits. See our guide to Tanzania park fees for the other northern parks if you plan a safari afterwards.

What a bigger group saves, and what it does not

On a Kilimanjaro group climb, fixed costs such as the vehicle to the gate, the lead guide's wages and the kitchen tent are split between more people as a group grows. Per-person costs such as park fees, food, porters to carry each climber's kit and sleeping bag hire stay the same. The saving is real but smaller than many organisers hope, and it levels off once a group passes about eight people because extra guides and a second mess tent are needed.

How Should a Group Train and Prepare for the Altitude?

A group should start training together about three to four months before the climb, building up to back-to-back long walks with a loaded daypack. Fitness helps, but it does not protect anyone from altitude sickness, so acclimatisation days matter more than gym sessions.

Photo: Divulge Adventures

The NHS advice on altitude sickness is a useful shared reference for everyone on a Kilimanjaro group climb. Above 3,000 m it recommends not sleeping more than 500 m higher than the night before and taking a rest day every three to four days. Symptoms such as headache, nausea and poor sleep usually start 6 to 10 hours after arriving at a new height, and anyone whose symptoms get worse should descend. Ask everyone to speak to their GP or a travel clinic about preventive medicine, and read our post on altitude sickness on the Machame route for what it feels like on the mountain.

A simple training timeline for a Kilimanjaro group climb

Months three and four before departure: two or three walks a week, with one long weekend hike. Month two: add hills, stairs and a full day out in the boots you will climb in. The final month: a back-to-back weekend of two long days, then ease off in the last ten days. Training walks before a Kilimanjaro group climb also show the organiser early who might need a longer route.

When should the group climb?

The driest months are January to mid-March and June to October. Our month-by-month guide to climbing Kilimanjaro explains how each month feels on the mountain, which matters when you are fixing dates for a Kilimanjaro group climb and many people cannot easily move them.

Summit Night: How Does a Group Stay Together, or Split Safely?

On summit night a group leaves high camp around midnight and climbs in single file behind the lead guide. If anyone slows badly or feels unwell, an assistant guide stays with them while the others continue, so the plan must allow for splitting from the start.

Photo by Daniel Vargas on Unsplash

On the Machame and Lemosho routes the summit push starts from Barafu Camp at about 4,670 m and climbs to Stella Point on the crater rim before Uhuru Peak. It is cold, dark and slow. On a Kilimanjaro group climb, those who agree the rules beforehand cope far better: the guide's call on turning back is final, nobody argues to keep a struggling friend going, and those who summit do not need to wait at the top.

Agree the rules before you leave home

Write down three things and share them with the group: who decides when someone turns back (the guide), what happens to the rest of the group (they continue with the other guides), and how success is measured. Some groups, charity climbs especially, choose to count reaching high camp or Stella Point as the shared goal, with Uhuru Peak as the bonus.

Private Kilimanjaro Group Climb or Joining an Open Departure?

A private Kilimanjaro group climb is better when you already have four or more people, because you choose the dates, route and pace yourselves. Joining an open departure suits individuals and couples, but you share the mountain with strangers whose fitness and goals may differ from yours.

On a private Kilimanjaro group climb you also control the details that matter on a long climb: dietary needs, a later wake-up on rest days, a celebration dinner in Moshi, a company banner at the summit sign. You can add a safari afterwards too, for example to the Serengeti or Ngorongoro, without fitting around other people's plans. Our group safaris page explains how we plan trips for clubs, charities and companies, and the step-by-step guide to organising a group safari works just as well for a climb.

Group Organiser's Checklist

  • Deposits: collect them early and set a clear cancellation rule so one drop-out does not change everyone's price
  • Insurance: check every climber's policy covers trekking to 6,000 m and helicopter evacuation
  • Medical forms: gather them privately and share only what the lead guide needs to know
  • Tipping: agree a pooled tip fund before the climb and know the exact crew number
  • Kit list: send one shared list and hold a gear check in Moshi the evening before
  • Rooming: fix tent pairs before departure, not at the gate
  • Recovery day: keep a spare night in Moshi after the climb for slow descents or delayed flights

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the best group size for a Kilimanjaro group climb?

The best size for a Kilimanjaro group climb is usually four to twelve people: large enough to share fixed costs, small enough for guides to watch everyone closely. Larger groups work too, but they are best split into two crews walking a few minutes apart, each with its own lead guide.

Can everyone in a group reach the summit of Kilimanjaro?

Not always. Altitude affects people differently, regardless of fitness, so a Kilimanjaro group climb should be planned on the assumption that someone may need to turn back. Choosing a longer route of eight days on the mountain gives the best odds for everyone, and adding enough guides means one climber descending never ends the summit attempt for the rest.

How much are Kilimanjaro park fees for a group?

Kilimanjaro park fees are charged per person, so a group pays the same rate per climber as a solo trekker. For adult non-residents the conservation fee is US$70 a day, camping US$50 a night and the rescue fee US$20 per trip, with 18% VAT added (checked November 2026). Savings in a group come from shared transport, guides and kitchen crew, not from the fees.

Which Kilimanjaro route is best for a group?

For most groups the Lemosho route over eight days on the mountain is the best choice, because it gains height slowly and gives the widest margin for mixed fitness levels. Machame suits fitter groups short on time, Rongai suits groups wanting quieter trails and a drier northern side, and Marangu is the only route with huts instead of tents.

Should we tip the crew together on a Kilimanjaro group climb?

Most groups pool tips into one fund, agreed before the climb, then hand them out at a ceremony on the final day. The Kilimanjaro Porters Assistance Project recommends knowing the exact crew size in advance and giving each crew member an individual envelope, so every porter receives their share directly rather than through someone else.

Final Thoughts

A successful Kilimanjaro group climb comes from three early choices: a long enough route, enough guides to split the group safely, and rules everyone agrees before they fly. Get those right and the fees, kit and tipping fall into place. Send us your numbers and dates, and we will build your Kilimanjaro group climb around the people in it.
